findings.problem: Reads like flat, generic quiz feedback ('Egypt is a fair guess... But this text points somewhere else') with none of Papa Dorin's voice or humor.
States that 'Moab is where Elimelech's family settles' without citing Ruth 1:2, since Ruth 1:1 does not name Elimelech or say they settled.
Flat and generic ('sounds like a solid pick, friend, but it's not the one the text gives'), lacking Papa Dorin's personality or humor.
Mild and generic ('She walks in quietly here, and she ends up in the middle of the whole story') instead of bringing Papa Dorin's energy and humor.
Flat and teacher-like ('Rachel is a real Bible name... Stay with those two names, friend') with no humor or distinct Papa Dorin voice.
Flat and repetitive ('Dinah is a name from another part of the Bible... Ruth is the one to hang on to'), missing Papa Dorin's personality.
States 'Back at the start of the story there was a famine' as a Bible fact without citing Ruth 1:1.
Flat and generic ('A king is a big piece of news, friend, but it's not what Naomi hears') with no real humor.
Flat and generic ('Victory would make for a different kind of story'), missing a chance for Papa Dorin's humor.
Completely dry response to a silly distractor ('Walk faster to beat the dark'), missing an easy opportunity for Papa Dorin to be funny.
States 'The two of them have just started the road with her' without citing Ruth 1:7.
Flat and dry ('That's the opposite of what Naomi says...'), lacking Papa Dorin's voice.

Says 'She's praying for good things for both of them,' whereas Ruth 1:9 shows Naomi speaking a wish/blessing to her daughters-in-law, not praying (breaks the rule to call things what the text calls them).

Says 'She's asking the LORD to bless each of them with rest and a new home,' which directly breaks the rule and example in papa-dorin.md under 'Call things what the text calls them' ('Naomi asks the LORD to bless them' vs. 'Naomi tells them, "May the LORD..."').
Very flat and bare ('That's it... They want to stay with her') with no Papa Dorin personality.
Flat and generic ('That's not what they say, friend. They don't offer to wait around') with no humor.
Flat and mild ('A visit sounds nice, but that's not their offer'), missing Papa Dorin's comic energy.
States 'She wants them to see how things really stand before they decide' as fact, adding an unstated inner motive/desire without marking it as his own guess ('I think').
Flat and dry, missing the humor in Naomi's impossible hypothetical question.
Flat and dry ('Naomi doesn't ask that one, friend. She asks about waiting') with no Papa Dorin humor.
Flat and generic ('That's not Naomi's question. She isn't sending them on ahead') with no personality or humor.
Flat and teacher-like ('This is Orpah, not Ruth, so keep them straight, friend') without Papa Dorin's warmth or humor.
Dry and plain ('There were tears first, then a kiss, and then she goes') with no distinct Papa Dorin voice.
Flat and plain ('Not this time. Ruth doesn't go back with Orpah') with no personality or humor.
Reads like a dry reading-comprehension note ('That little word "but" tells you the two of them part ways') rather than Papa Dorin.
Flat and repetitive ('She's still trying to send Ruth home. She's said it before, and she says it again') with no humor or distinct voice.
Flat and plain ('Naomi hasn't given up yet. She tells Ruth to go after Orpah'), lacking Papa Dorin's personality.
States 'Orpah went back to her gods' as narrator fact without citing Ruth 1:15 (where Naomi says this to Ruth).
Flat and bare ('Ruth doesn't promise that, friend. Her promise is about people and God') with no Papa Dorin voice.
Flat and generic ('That's not part of her promise. Ruth says something bigger') with no distinct personality.
Flat summary ('She has argued with Ruth and sent her home more than once. Now Naomi lets it rest') with none of Papa Dorin's humor or punch.
Flat and dry ('Naomi already tried that, friend, and it didn't work'), missing Papa Dorin's comic timing.
Robotic and bare ('That's not what happens. Naomi doesn't tell Ruth to wait anywhere') with zero Papa Dorin voice.
States 'and they were shocked' as a fact about the women's feelings without marking it as Papa Dorin's own guess ('I think' or 'I bet').
